I'm conflicted. On the one hand, I believe that bringing well preserved corpses back from the dead is possible in theory. If I had money to spare, well, its worth a gamble.

On the other hand, I see severe sequencing constraints. In the novel Glass House, by Charlie Stross, nano-technology can disassemble people in real time. Long distance travel is done using Assembler Gates that take your molecules apart, atom by atom, transmit data at the speed of light, then print "you" out at the far destination. The printing out part is crucial to the resurrection dream. Scan in the frozen corpse. Use lots of computer power to do computational medicine. Print out the resurrected feral-toes. Glass house is set eleven thousand years into the future. That might not be long enough!

But what do I mean by sequencing constraints? I'm thinking that amazing technology develops step by step. A hundred years at wow-level-one, a hundred years at wow-level-two,... after 11,000 years technology reaches wow-level-one-hundred-and-ten and starts reviving frozen corpses.

Think about the early stuff, spelling out the letters IBM using Xenon atoms. It was cryogenic. Nano-technology will likely stay cryogenic for centuries; you can print amazing stuff, but it has to be thawable: print it out at 10 Kelvin and bring it up to room temperature over a few hours. Nano-technology will likely stay microscopic for centuries. Start with printing out viruses for phage therapy. Move on to bacteria for industrial processes. Move on to mammalian cells, such as stem cells for rejuvenation therapies. Nano-technology will likely stay slow for centuries. It might take a month to print a stem cell. Let it multiply, inject it, feel twenty years younger.

Before technology gets to the point of warm, fast, macroscopic nano-technology suitable for printing out revived people, there will be several centuries of cryogenic, slow, microscopic nano-technology. Cryogenic, slow, microscopic nano-technology is enough for germ-line therapies and the transition to the post-human era. Post-human with a health span of 700 years and an IQ of 700. I said earlier "I believe that bringing well preserved corpses back from the dead is possible in theory" but I don't believe that mankind will actually go down that path. Well before it becomes technically possible, other, lesser, but still dazzling possibilities will seduce mankind. Post-humans will over-come the fear of death through better genetics and rejuvenation therapy. Attempting to revive 21st century humans will seem bizarre and cruel; where could they possibly fit in a post-human future?

On the third hand, the orthodox view is that if you are revived in the far future, you will be revived to live in a world of unlimited medical power and get to enjoy physical immortality. The orthodox view is that this is a huge prize, well worth pursuing.

Personally, I'm not too convinced about the fixity of the soul. I think that I'm 99% the person I was a year ago, and 1% new and different. I can look forward to 99% survival into being next years feral-toes. But the drift accumulates year on year. When I think about how much I care about the feral-toes of 2118, I raise the annual decay rate 0.99 to the power of 100 and conclude that he is 36.6% me, 63.4% somebody else. Immortality gives a lot of extra years of life, but to a succession of different people. Summing the geometric series to infinity it gives a hundred extra years of life to me. So I'm luke warm on personal immortality.
